extracted.intended_audience: journalists and newsroom staff (reporters, social media editors, verification trainers)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide for journalists on how to verify online content (photos, videos, social posts) using repeatable checks, tools and investigative techniques. Emphasises five core checks (provenance, source, date, location, motivation) plus documentation, safety and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute essentials — Is the content connected to a real event?
rubrics_metrics.description: Before verifying any content online, ask: Is the content I am looking at connected to an event that actually took place? The fundamental claim of the content should be the first thing you check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the core claim is false (e.g., a headline like “Pope Endorses Donald Trump”), other verification work may be secondary. Use news reports or other independent reporting to confirm an event occurred before deep-diving into provenance, source, date or location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the rabbit hole / Is this worth verifying?
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if the time and effort to verify a piece of content is justified by its reach or importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification often takes minutes but can become time-consuming; avoid obsessing over one hypothesis. Measure reach by shares/likes/retweets/views/comments where possible and consider not pursuing low-engagement content. Remember research showing debunks can amplify false claims; weigh the value of reporting a debunk against potential spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance — Identify the original piece of content
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you looking at the original account, article or piece of content? Provenance is the most important check and should usually be run first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding the original unlocks context and motivation; beware 'scrapes' (content downloaded and reuploaded elsewhere). Use reverse image search to locate older instances of photos/videos. If you find older versions presented as new, this signals potential repurposing or misleading context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse image search tools and methods (under Provenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reverse image search engines to find matching or similar images and older instances of visual media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Google Images: useful 'Pages that include matching images' and custom date ranges (but cannot sort by date). Yandex: large database; can find faces and flipped images. TinEye: lets you sort results by date to see first recorded instance but has a smaller database. Recommended extension: RevEye (Chrome/Firefox) to run multiple engines quickly. For videos, screenshot a frame and run reverse image searches on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video verification and InVID
rubrics_metrics.description: Video provenance can be found by breaking videos into thumbnails and searching frames; use InVID Verification Plugin for many video verification tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: InVID can: break videos into thumbnails for reverse image searching; show upload date/time and account data; extract verification-related comments using NLP; provide a magnifying tool to inspect small text. For videos, start with the thumbnail/first frame and reverse search it. Use InVID to get upload metadata (UTC) and other clues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check anonymous and closed spaces for earlier versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinformation and memes often originate in closed or anonymous spaces; search there for earlier instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search Reddit (native search), 4chan/archived 4chan (4chansearch.com), Gab.ai and, where feasible and safe, Discord channels, Facebook groups and WhatsApp groups. These spaces may be harder to search but can reveal origin points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source — identify who captured the original content (primary source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between who posted a piece of content and who captured it; the primary source is the person who captured it and is ideally the person to identify and contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Who is the uploader? Could they have reuploaded someone else’s material? Does their account history make sense for being near the event? Look for contact information to speak directly to the source before making identity claims. Use reverse image searches on profile photos, search for identical text/language across accounts, look up usernames, and check LinkedIn or associated websites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigating accounts and bot/cyborg detection (under Source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether an account is automated or human-operated and whether it consistently spreads misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bot forensics is imprecise: tools that flag high tweeting rates (e.g., 50 tweets/day) can misclassify active humans. Consider circadian activity (periods of silence for sleep) as a signal. Be aware of 'cyborgs' (accounts that mix automation and human activity) and that the relevant issue is whether the account amplifies misinformation. Tools: Hoaxy, BotSentinel (with caution). Use Twitonomy to analyze tweet history, join date, average tweets/day, retweet patterns, replies, hashtags and top interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigating domains and registrant information
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate website ownership, hosting, historical records and related domains to assess site authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools: viewDNS.info for domain/IP searches, reverse IP to see other sites on the same server, and historical IP addresses. If registrant data is hidden (GDPR-protected), check old versions of the site or variations (.net, .info). Paid directories like Spokeo and Pipl can help find contact information. Look for suspicious URL endings and evidence of migration or obfuscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date — determine when content was captured (not just uploaded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify when content was created/captured, not merely when it was uploaded to a platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform timestamps show upload time; stronger verification aims to find capture time. Use Exif metadata if you can obtain an original file (many social platforms strip Exif on upload). Tools and techniques: Jeffrey’s Exif Viewer for metadata; InVID to view upload times for videos (UTC); SunCalc to check sun angles for time-of-day clues; Wolfram Alpha to check historical weather. Always verify provenance first and use reverse image search to find older instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exif and file metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspect file metadata (Exif) for timestamps, device information and coordinates when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exif data can include time, date, camera settings and GPS coordinates, but platforms often remove Exif on upload. Ask uploaders for the original file via email to access Exif. Be aware metadata can be faked by sophisticated actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location — verify where content was captured
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm the geographic location where an image, video or post was captured rather than relying solely on platform geotags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geotags and metadata can be wrong or manipulated. Independently verify by cross-referencing map/satellite imagery and street view. Observe unique geographic features, buildings, signage, license plates, telephone numbers, weather and foliage. Use Google Maps, Google Earth (historical satellite), Bing, Yandex (good for Eastern Europe), and Wikimapia. Combine multiple clues (e.g., area code + cell tower + building features) to triangulate locations. Note that satellite imagery can be out of date after rapid landscape changes (e.g., disasters, war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation — understand why content was captured or posted
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek to determine the purpose behind capturing or posting content (propaganda, activism, eyewitnessing, corporate/government motive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation is difficult to verify; the best approach is to ask the source. Ask whether the uploader was an accidental eyewitness, an activist, attending to capture a particular perspective, affiliated with institutions, or part of online communities promoting a cause. Use profile behavior to infer likely motives but avoid overclaiming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document it — preserve evidence and maintain transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Record and save evidence as you investigate because content can be deleted or altered, and documentation supports transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screenshot everything (explain how-to on Mac/Windows), use screen-grabbing tools (Evernote), save pages with the Wayback Machine extension, and consider paid tools like Hunch.ly for automated documentation of browser activity. Documenting aids transparency and protects against loss of crucial information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set up a verification toolbox and monitoring workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Build and maintain a personal toolbox of verification resources and monitoring systems to work efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bookmark systems or Start.me as a hub for tools. Keep the toolbox updated because platforms and tools change. For concurrent monitoring, set up dashboards (e.g., TweetDeck columns) and alerts using keywords from the item under investigation; maintain lists of accounts that often engage with the source to surface related content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staying safe — personal digital security during investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt basic and enhanced digital-security practices, especially when working in closed/anonymous spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a password manager, review your own digital footprint and privacy settings, consider a VPN and anonymous browsers (Tor), limit personal information shared in closed spaces, and be cautious about exposing others’ data. If posting information from closed spaces, be mindful of operational security and the potential risk to sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and journalistic standards still apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional journalism ethics (accuracy, minimizing harm, consent) apply to digital verification and may introduce new considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct interviews over quoting online posts. Avoid needlessly prying into private lives; understand screenshotting implicates real people and secure your systems to avoid leaking sensitive data. Be transparent about your purpose if participating in closed/anonymous spaces. See First Draft guides for deeper ethical guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elusiveness of certainty — be transparent about what you know and don’t know
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital verification rarely yields absolute certainty; treat it as detective work that assembles corroborating clues rather than definitive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect as much corroborating evidence as possible, but acknowledge uncertainty in reporting. Use a detective-board approach to show connections between clues and be forthright with audiences about unresolved questions.
